newsitem.title: INDIA: India's forgotten children have little to celebrate.
newsitem.headline: India's forgotten children have little to celebrate.

text.p: India will celebrate 50 years of independence at midnight on Thursday, but millions of forgotten child labourers will still be waiting for their dawn of freedom.
Shouting for an end to child labour, hundreds of children marched through the wide avenues of New Delhi on Thursday as the nation prepared to celebrate its Golden Jubilee.
Arriving at parliament, the children presented a memorandum to the nation's president demanding that all children should receive an education and that no child should be forced to work.
Many of the children themselves had only recently been freed from bonded labour and poignantly asked the question earlier: What did independence mean for them?

The march to parliament marked the culmination of a two-day meeting on the problem of child labour in South Asia. Earlier on Thursday, the children sat in a semi-circle in the shadow of the Old Fort in New Delhi in a self-styled parliament.
They condemned the government for not delivering to them their basic constitutional right of a free education for every child under 14.
Govind, 14, a ragged but enthusiastic boy delighted in his temporary position of "Speaker of the House."
"We are the children who are the future of this country," he said. "We are the ones who earn the nation's income, but what do we have to celebrate?"
"Fifty years ago we won our freedom from the British. Today, child labourers are still the slaves of the Indians who speak English," Govind continued.
One by one, the children had their turn to address the assembly. They all told a common story of exploitation, abuse, poverty and misery.
Child activist Satish Kalyarthi of the South Asian Coalition for Child Servitude spoke of the scale of the problem of child labour in the sub-continent.

"There are more than 60 million child labourers in South Asia," he said. "What is lacking is the political will and social concern to implement the provisions of the Constitution and the 1986 Child Labour Act."
The Indian government disputes Kalyarthi's figures. According to the Indian Labour Ministry, only 18 million children are employed in labour-intensive industries.
India officially banned the employment of children under 14 in 1948 and outlawed child labour in 17 hazardous industries under the 1986 act.

Under India's 1950 constitution, the state committed itself to provide free and compulsory education for all children up to 14 within 10 years. The Supreme Court, in a landmark decision, upheld this constitutional right in 1993.

The country is also party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which it ratified in 1992. Under this treaty, India undertook to make primary education compulsory and free to all.
As night fell, the rally came to a close. Thousands of candles were lit to mark the beginning of a new era.
"The children are tired of hollow promises from the politicians," Kalyarthi said. "They will continue their struggle against child labour until every child in India is free."
